| Date | Development |
| --- | --- |
| Early 1970s | Jane Robinson and Don Walker established an influential [Natural Language Processing](/wiki/Natural_Language_Processing "Natural Language Processing") group at SRI.[[73]](#cite_note-75) |
| 1970 | [Seppo Linnainmaa](/wiki/Seppo_Linnainmaa "Seppo Linnainmaa") publishes the reverse mode of [automatic differentiation](/wiki/Automatic_differentiation "Automatic differentiation"). This method became later known as [backpropagation](/wiki/Backpropagation "Backpropagation"), and is heavily used to train [artificial neural networks](/wiki/Artificial_neural_networks "Artificial neural networks").[[74]](#cite_note-76) |
| Jaime Carbonell (Sr.) developed SCHOLAR, an interactive program for [computer assisted instruction](/wiki/Computer_assisted_instruction "Computer assisted instruction") based on semantic nets as the representation of knowledge. |
| Bill Woods described Augmented Transition Networks (ATN's) as a representation for natural language understanding. |
| [Patrick Winston](/wiki/Patrick_Winston "Patrick Winston")'s PhD program, ARCH, at MIT learned concepts from examples in the world of children's blocks. |
| 1971 | [Terry Winograd](/wiki/Terry_Winograd "Terry Winograd")'s PhD thesis ([MIT](/wiki/MIT "MIT")) demonstrated the ability of computers to understand English sentences in a restricted world of children's blocks, in a coupling of his language understanding program, [SHRDLU](/wiki/SHRDLU "SHRDLU"), with a robot arm that carried out instructions typed in English. |
| Work on the Boyer-Moore theorem prover started in [Edinburgh](/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh").[[75]](#cite_note-77) |
| 1972 | [Prolog](/wiki/Prolog "Prolog") programming language developed by [Alain Colmerauer](/wiki/Alain_Colmerauer "Alain Colmerauer"). |
| Earl Sacerdoti developed one of the first hierarchical planning programs, ABSTRIPS. |
| 1973 | The Assembly Robotics Group at [University of Edinburgh](/wiki/University_of_Edinburgh "University of Edinburgh") builds Freddy Robot, capable of using [visual perception](/wiki/Visual_perception "Visual perception") to locate and assemble models. (See [Edinburgh *Freddy* Assembly Robot](/wiki/Freddy_II "Freddy II"): a versatile computer-controlled assembly system.) |
| The [Lighthill report](/wiki/Lighthill_report "Lighthill report") gives a largely negative verdict on AI research in Great Britain and forms the basis for the decision by the British government to discontinue support for AI research in all but two universities. |
| 1974 | [Ted Shortliffe](/wiki/Edward_H._Shortliffe "Edward H. Shortliffe")'s PhD dissertation on the [MYCIN](/wiki/MYCIN "MYCIN") program (Stanford) demonstrated a very practical rule-based approach to medical diagnoses, even in the presence of uncertainty. While it borrowed from DENDRAL, its own contributions strongly influenced the future of [expert system](/wiki/Expert_system "Expert system") development, especially commercial systems. |
| 1975 | Earl Sacerdoti developed techniques of [partial-order planning](/wiki/Partial-order_planning "Partial-order planning") in his NOAH system, replacing the previous paradigm of search among state space descriptions. NOAH was applied at SRI International to interactively diagnose and repair electromechanical systems. |
| [Austin Tate](/wiki/Austin_Tate "Austin Tate") developed the Nonlin hierarchical planning system able to search a space of [partial plans](/wiki/Partial_plan "Partial plan") characterised as alternative approaches to the underlying goal structure of the plan. |
| Marvin Minsky published his widely read and influential article on [Frames](/wiki/Frame_problem "Frame problem") as a representation of knowledge, in which many ideas about [schemas](/wiki/Schema_(psychology) "Schema (psychology)") and [semantic links](/wiki/Semantic_link "Semantic link") are brought together. |
| The Meta-Dendral learning program produced new results in [chemistry](/wiki/Chemistry "Chemistry") (some rules of [mass spectrometry](/wiki/Mass_spectrometry "Mass spectrometry")) the first scientific discoveries by a computer to be published in a refereed journal. |
| Mid-1970s | [Barbara Grosz](/wiki/Barbara_Grosz "Barbara Grosz") (SRI) established limits to traditional AI approaches to discourse modeling. Subsequent work by Grosz, [Bonnie Webber](/wiki/Bonnie_Webber "Bonnie Webber") and [Candace Sidner](/wiki/Candace_Sidner "Candace Sidner") developed the notion of "centering", used in establishing focus of [discourse](/wiki/Discourse "Discourse") and anaphoric references in [Natural language processing](/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing"). |
| [David Marr](/wiki/David_Marr_(psychologist) "David Marr (psychologist)") and [MIT](/wiki/MIT "MIT") colleagues describe the "primal sketch" and its role in [visual perception](/wiki/Visual_perception "Visual perception"). |
| 1976 | [Douglas Lenat](/wiki/Douglas_Lenat "Douglas Lenat")'s [AM program](/wiki/Automated_Mathematician "Automated Mathematician") (Stanford PhD dissertation) demonstrated the discovery model (loosely guided search for interesting conjectures). |
| Randall Davis demonstrated the power of meta-level reasoning in his PhD dissertation at Stanford. |
| Stevo Bozinovski and Ante Fulgosi introduced transfer learning method in artificial intelligence, based on the psychology of learning.[[76]](#cite_note-78)[[77]](#cite_note-79) |
| 1978 | [Tom Mitchell](/wiki/Tom_M._Mitchell "Tom M. Mitchell"), at Stanford, invented the concept of [Version spaces](/wiki/Version_space "Version space") for describing the [search space](/wiki/Candidate_solution "Candidate solution") of a concept formation program. |
| [Herbert A. Simon](/wiki/Herbert_A._Simon "Herbert A. Simon") wins the [Nobel Prize in Economics](/wiki/Bank_of_Sweden_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences_in_Memory_of_Alfred_Nobel "Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel") for his theory of [bounded rationality](/wiki/Bounded_rationality "Bounded rationality"), one of the cornerstones of AI known as "[satisficing](/wiki/Satisficing "Satisficing")". |
| The MOLGEN program, written at [Stanford](/wiki/Stamford,_Connecticut "Stamford, Connecticut") by Mark Stefik and Peter Friedland, demonstrated that an [object-oriented programming](/wiki/Object-oriented_programming "Object-oriented programming") representation of knowledge can be used to plan gene-[cloning](/wiki/Cloning "Cloning") experiments. |
| 1979 | Bill VanMelle's PhD dissertation at Stanford demonstrated the generality of [MYCIN](/wiki/MYCIN "MYCIN")'s representation of knowledge and style of reasoning in his [EMYCIN](/w/index.php?title=EMYCIN&action=edit&redlink=1 "EMYCIN (page does not exist)") program, the model for many commercial expert system "shells". |
| Jack Myers and Harry Pople at [University of Pittsburgh](/wiki/University_of_Pittsburgh "University of Pittsburgh") developed INTERNIST, a knowledge-based medical diagnosis program based on Dr. Myers' [clinical](/wiki/Clinic "Clinic") knowledge. |
| [Cordell Green](/wiki/Cordell_Green "Cordell Green"), David Barstow, [Elaine Kant](/wiki/Elaine_Kant "Elaine Kant") and others at Stanford demonstrated the CHI system for [automatic programming](/wiki/Automatic_programming "Automatic programming"). |
| The Stanford Cart, built by [Hans Moravec](/wiki/Hans_Moravec "Hans Moravec"), becomes the first computer-controlled, [autonomous vehicle](/wiki/Autonomous_robot "Autonomous robot") when it successfully traverses a chair-filled room and circumnavigates the [Stanford AI Lab](/wiki/Stanford_AI_Lab "Stanford AI Lab"). |
| BKG, a backgammon program written by [Hans Berliner](/wiki/Hans_Berliner "Hans Berliner") at [CMU](/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University"), defeats the reigning world champion (in part via luck). |
| Drew McDermott and Jon Doyle at [MIT](/wiki/MIT "MIT"), and John McCarthy at Stanford begin publishing work on [non-monotonic logics](/wiki/Non-monotonic_logic "Non-monotonic logic") and formal aspects of truth maintenance. |
| Late 1970s | Stanford's SUMEX-AIM resource, headed by Ed Feigenbaum and Joshua Lederberg, demonstrates the power of the ARPAnet for scientific collaboration. |

| 1980s | [Lisp machines](/wiki/Lisp_machine "Lisp machine") developed and marketed. First [expert system](/wiki/Expert_system "Expert system") shells and commercial applications. |
| 1980 | First National Conference of the [American Association for Artificial Intelligence](/wiki/American_Association_for_Artificial_Intelligence "American Association for Artificial Intelligence") (AAAI) held at Stanford. |
| 1981 | [Danny Hillis](/wiki/Danny_Hillis "Danny Hillis") designs the connection machine, which utilizes [parallel computing](/wiki/Parallel_computing "Parallel computing") to bring new power to AI, and to computation in general. (Later founds [Thinking Machines Corporation](/wiki/Thinking_Machines_Corporation "Thinking Machines Corporation")) |
| Stevo Bozinovski and Charles Anderson carry out first concurrent programming (task parallelism) in neural network research. A program, "CAA Controller" written and executed by Bozinovski interacts with the program "Inverted Pendulum Dynamics" written and executed by Anderson, using VAX/VMS mailboxes as a way of inter-program communication. The CAA controller learns to balance the simulated inverted pendulum.[[78]](#cite_note-80)[[79]](#cite_note-81)[[80]](#cite_note-82) |
| 1982 | The [Fifth Generation Computer Systems project](/wiki/Fifth_Generation_Computer_Systems_project "Fifth Generation Computer Systems project") (FGCS), an initiative by Japan's [Ministry of International Trade and Industry](/wiki/Ministry_of_International_Trade_and_Industry "Ministry of International Trade and Industry"), begun in 1982, to create a "fifth generation computer" (see history of computing hardware) which was supposed to perform much calculation utilizing massive parallelism. |
| 1983 | John Laird and Paul Rosenbloom, working with [Allen Newell](/wiki/Allen_Newell "Allen Newell"), complete CMU dissertations on [Soar](/wiki/Soar_(cognitive_architecture) "Soar (cognitive architecture)") (program). |
| [James F. Allen](/wiki/James_F._Allen_(computer_scientist) "James F. Allen (computer scientist)") invents the Interval Calculus, the first widely used formalization of temporal events. |
| Mid-1980s | Neural Networks become widely used with the [Backpropagation](/wiki/Backpropagation "Backpropagation") [algorithm](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm"), also known as the reverse mode of [automatic differentiation](/wiki/Automatic_differentiation "Automatic differentiation") published by [Seppo Linnainmaa](/wiki/Seppo_Linnainmaa "Seppo Linnainmaa") in 1970 and applied to neural networks by [Paul Werbos](/wiki/Paul_Werbos "Paul Werbos"). |
| 1985 | The autonomous drawing program, [AARON](/wiki/AARON "AARON"), created by [Harold Cohen](/wiki/Harold_Cohen_(artist) "Harold Cohen (artist)"), is demonstrated at the AAAI National Conference (based on more than a decade of work, and with subsequent work showing major developments). |
| 1986 | The team of [Ernst Dickmanns](/wiki/Ernst_Dickmanns "Ernst Dickmanns") at [Bundeswehr University of Munich](/wiki/Bundeswehr_University_of_Munich "Bundeswehr University of Munich") builds the first robot cars, driving up to 55 mph on empty streets. |
| [Barbara Grosz](/wiki/Barbara_Grosz "Barbara Grosz") and [Candace Sidner](/wiki/Candace_Sidner "Candace Sidner") create the first computation model of [discourse](/wiki/Discourse "Discourse"), establishing the field of research.[[81]](#cite_note-83) |
| 1987 | Marvin Minsky published *[The Society of Mind](/wiki/The_Society_of_Mind "The Society of Mind")*, a theoretical description of the mind as a collection of cooperating [agents](/wiki/Intelligent_agent "Intelligent agent"). He had been lecturing on the idea for years before the book came out (cf. Doyle 1983).[[82]](#cite_note-Henderson2007-84) |
| Around the same time, [Rodney Brooks](/wiki/Rodney_Brooks "Rodney Brooks") introduced the [subsumption architecture](/wiki/Subsumption_architecture "Subsumption architecture") and [behavior-based robotics](/wiki/Behavior-based_robotics "Behavior-based robotics") as a more minimalist modular model of natural intelligence; [Nouvelle AI](/wiki/Nouvelle_AI "Nouvelle AI"). |
| Commercial launch of generation 2.0 of Alacrity by Alacritous Inc./Allstar Advice Inc. Toronto, the first commercial strategic and managerial advisory system. The system was based upon a forward-chaining, self-developed expert system with 3,000 rules about the evolution of markets and competitive strategies and co-authored by Alistair Davidson and Mary Chung, founders of the firm with the underlying engine developed by Paul Tarvydas. The Alacrity system also included a small financial expert system that interpreted financial statements and models.[[83]](#cite_note-85) |
| 1989 | The development of [metal–oxide–semiconductor](/wiki/Metal%E2%80%93oxide%E2%80%93semiconductor "Metal–oxide–semiconductor") (MOS) [Very-large-scale integration](/wiki/Very-large-scale_integration "Very-large-scale integration") (VLSI), in the form of [complementary MOS](/wiki/CMOS "CMOS") (CMOS) technology, enabled the development of practical [artificial neural network](/wiki/Neural_network_(machine_learning) "Neural network (machine learning)") (ANN) technology in the 1980s. A landmark publication in the field was the 1989 book *Analog VLSI Implementation of Neural Systems* by Carver A. Mead and Mohammed Ismail.[[84]](#cite_note-Mead-86) |
| Dean Pomerleau at CMU creates ALVINN (An Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network), which was used in the [Navlab](/wiki/Navlab "Navlab") program. |

| 1990s | Major advances in all areas of AI, with significant demonstrations in machine learning, [intelligent tutoring](/wiki/Computer_assisted_instruction "Computer assisted instruction"), case-based reasoning, multi-agent planning, [scheduling](/wiki/Scheduling_(computing) "Scheduling (computing)"), uncertain reasoning, [data mining](/wiki/Data_mining "Data mining"), natural language understanding and translation, vision, [virtual reality](/wiki/Virtual_reality "Virtual reality"), games, and other topics. |
| Early 1990s | [TD-Gammon](/wiki/TD-Gammon "TD-Gammon"), a [backgammon](/wiki/Backgammon "Backgammon") program written by Gerry Tesauro, demonstrates that [reinforcement](/wiki/Reinforcement "Reinforcement") (learning) is powerful enough to create a championship-level game-playing program by competing favorably with world-class players. |
| 1991 | [DART](/wiki/Dynamic_Analysis_and_Replanning_Tool "Dynamic Analysis and Replanning Tool") scheduling application deployed in the first [Gulf War](/wiki/Gulf_War "Gulf War") paid back [DARPA's](/wiki/DARPA "DARPA") investment of 30 years in AI research.[[85]](#cite_note-87) |
| 1992 | [Carol Stoker](/w/index.php?title=Carol_Stoker&action=edit&redlink=1 "Carol Stoker (page does not exist)") and NASA Ames robotics team explore marine life in Antarctica with an undersea robot [Telepresence](/wiki/Telepresence "Telepresence") [ROV](/wiki/Remotely_Operated_Vehicle "Remotely Operated Vehicle") operated from the ice near McMurdo Bay, Antarctica and remotely via satellite link from Moffett Field, California.[[86]](#cite_note-88) |
| 1993 | [Ian Horswill](/w/index.php?title=Ian_Horswill&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ian Horswill (page does not exist)") extended [behavior-based robotics](/wiki/Behavior-based_robotics "Behavior-based robotics") by creating Polly, the first robot to navigate using [vision](/wiki/Computer_vision "Computer vision") and operate at animal-like speeds (1 meter/second). |
| [Rodney Brooks](/wiki/Rodney_Brooks "Rodney Brooks"), [Lynn Andrea Stein](/w/index.php?title=Lynn_Andrea_Stein&action=edit&redlink=1 "Lynn Andrea Stein (page does not exist)") and [Cynthia Breazeal](/wiki/Cynthia_Breazeal "Cynthia Breazeal") started the widely publicized [MIT Cog project](/wiki/MIT_Cog_project "MIT Cog project") with numerous collaborators, in an attempt to build a [humanoid robot](/wiki/Humanoid_robot "Humanoid robot") child in just five years. |
| ISX corporation wins "DARPA contractor of the year"[[87]](#cite_note-89) for the [Dynamic Analysis and Replanning Tool](/wiki/Dynamic_Analysis_and_Replanning_Tool "Dynamic Analysis and Replanning Tool") (DART) which reportedly repaid the US government's entire investment in AI research since the 1950s.[[88]](#cite_note-90) |

| On March 7, 2023, *[Nature Biomedical Engineering](/wiki/Nature_Biomedical_Engineering "Nature Biomedical Engineering")* writes that "it is no longer possible to accurately distinguish" human-written text from text created by large language models, and that "It is all but certain that general-purpose large language models will rapidly proliferate... It is a rather safe bet that they will change many industries over time."[[153]](#cite_note-ZDTUM-155) |
| In response to ChatGPT, [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") releases in a limited capacity its chatbot [Google Bard](/wiki/Google_Bard "Google Bard"), based on the [LaMDA](/wiki/LaMDA "LaMDA") and [PaLM](/wiki/PaLM "PaLM") large language models, in March 2023.[[154]](#cite_note-156)[[155]](#cite_note-157) |
| On March 29, 2023, a petition of over 1,000 signatures is signed by Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak and other tech leaders, calling for a 6-month halt to what the petition refers to as "an out-of-control race" producing AI systems that its creators can not "understand, predict, or reliably control".[[156]](#cite_note-158)[[157]](#cite_note-159) |
| In May 2023, Google makes an announcement regarding Bard's transition from LaMDA to PaLM2, a significantly more advanced language model.[[158]](#cite_note-160) |
| In the last week of May 2023, a [Statement on AI Risk](/wiki/Statement_on_AI_risk_of_extinction "Statement on AI risk of extinction") is signed by [Geoffrey Hinton](/wiki/Geoffrey_Hinton "Geoffrey Hinton"), [Sam Altman](/wiki/Sam_Altman "Sam Altman"), [Bill Gates](/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates"), and many other prominent AI researchers and tech leaders with the following succinct message: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."[[159]](#cite_note-161)[[160]](#cite_note-162) |
| On July 9, 2023, [Sarah Silverman](/wiki/Sarah_Silverman "Sarah Silverman") files a class action lawsuit against Meta and OpenAI for copyright infringement for training their large language models on millions of authors' copyrighted works without permission.[[161]](#cite_note-163) |
| In August, 2023, the New York Times, CNN, Reuters, the Chicago Tribune, Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) and other news companies block OpenAI's GPTBot web crawler from accessing their content, while the New York Times also updates its terms of service to disallow the use of its content in large language models.[[162]](#cite_note-164) |
| On September 13, 2023, in a serious response to growing anxiety about the dangers of AI, the US Senate holds the inaugural bipartisan "[AI Insight Forum](/wiki/A.I._Insight_forums "A.I. Insight forums")", bringing together senators, CEOs, civil rights leaders and other industry reps, to further familiarize senators with the nature of AI and its risks, and to discuss needed safeguards and legislation.[[163]](#cite_note-AI_Legislation_Coming-165) The event is organized by Senate Majority Leader [Chuck Schumer](/wiki/Chuck_Schumer "Chuck Schumer") (D-NY),[[164]](#cite_note-NYTimes_Titans-166) and is chaired by U.S. Senator [Martin Heinrich](/wiki/Martin_Heinrich "Martin Heinrich") (D-N.M.), Founder and co-chair of the Senate AI Caucus.[[165]](#cite_note-167) Reflecting the importance of the meeting, the forum is attended by over 60 senators,[[166]](#cite_note-CNBC_Senate_AI_Forum-168) as well as [Elon Musk](/wiki/Elon_Musk "Elon Musk") (Tesla CEO), [Mark Zuckerberg](/wiki/Mark_Zuckerberg "Mark Zuckerberg") (Meta CEO), [Sam Altman](/wiki/Sam_Altman "Sam Altman") (OpenAI CEO), [Sundar Pichai](/wiki/Sundar_Pichai "Sundar Pichai") (Alphabet CEO), [Bill Gates](/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates") (Microsoft co-founder), [Satya Nadella](/wiki/Satya_Nadella "Satya Nadella") (Microsoft CEO), [Jensen Huang](/wiki/Jensen_Huang "Jensen Huang") (Nvidia CEO), [Arvind Krishna](/wiki/Arvind_Krishna "Arvind Krishna") (IBM CEO), [Alex Karp](/wiki/Alex_Karp "Alex Karp") (Palantir CEO), [Charles Rivkin](/wiki/Charles_Rivkin "Charles Rivkin") (chairman and CEO of the MPA), [Meredith Stiehm](/wiki/Meredith_Stiehm "Meredith Stiehm") (president of the Writers Guild of America West), [Liz Shuler](/wiki/Liz_Shuler "Liz Shuler") ([AFL-CIO](/wiki/AFL-CIO "AFL-CIO") President), and [Maya Wiley](/wiki/Maya_Wiley "Maya Wiley") (CEO of the [Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights](/wiki/Leadership_Conference_on_Civil_and_Human_Rights "Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights")), among others.[[163]](#cite_note-AI_Legislation_Coming-165)[[164]](#cite_note-NYTimes_Titans-166)[[166]](#cite_note-CNBC_Senate_AI_Forum-168) |
| In October 2023, AlpineGate AI Technologies Inc. CEO John Godel announced the launch of their AI Suite, AGImageAI, along with their proprietary GPT model, AlbertAGPT.[[167]](#cite_note-169) |
| On October 30, 2023, US President Biden signed the *[Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence](/wiki/Executive_Order_14110 "Executive Order 14110").*[[168]](#cite_note-170)[[169]](#cite_note-171) |
| In November 2023, the first global [AI Safety Summit](/wiki/2023_AI_Safety_Summit "2023 AI Safety Summit") was held in [Bletchley Park](/wiki/Bletchley_Park "Bletchley Park") in the UK to discuss the near and far term risks of AI and the possibility of mandatory and voluntary regulatory frameworks.[[170]](#cite_note-172) 28 countries including the United States, China, and the European Union issued a declaration at the start of the summit, calling for international co-operation to manage the challenges and risks of artificial intelligence.[[171]](#cite_note-2023-11-01-bletchley-declaration-full-173)[[172]](#cite_note-174) |
| [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") releases [Gemini](/wiki/Gemini_(language_model) "Gemini (language model)") 1.0 Ultra. |
| 2024 | On February 15, 2024, [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") releases [Gemini 1.5](/w/index.php?title=Gemini_1.5&action=edit&redlink=1 "Gemini 1.5 (page does not exist)") in limited beta, capable of context length up to 1 million tokens. |
| Also, on February 15, 2024, [OpenAI](/wiki/OpenAI "OpenAI") publicly announces [Sora](/wiki/Sora_(text-to-video_model) "Sora (text-to-video model)"), a text-to-video model for generating videos up to a minute long. |
| [Google DeepMind](/wiki/Google_DeepMind "Google DeepMind") unveils DNA prediction software AlphaFold which helps to identify cancer and genetic diseases. |
| On February 22, [StabilityAI](/wiki/Stability_AI "Stability AI") announces [Stable Diffusion](/wiki/Stable_Diffusion "Stable Diffusion") 3, using a similar architecture to [Sora](/wiki/Sora_(text-to-video_model) "Sora (text-to-video model)"). |
| On May 14, [Google](/wiki/Google "Google") adds an "AI overview" to Google searches. |
| On June 10, [Apple](/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.") announced "[Apple Intelligence](/wiki/Apple_Intelligence "Apple Intelligence")" which incorporates [ChatGPT](/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT") into new [iPhones](/wiki/IPhone "IPhone") and [Siri](/wiki/Siri "Siri"). |
| On October 9, co-founder and CEO of [Google DeepMind](/wiki/Google_DeepMind "Google DeepMind") and [Isomorphic Labs](/wiki/Isomorphic_Labs "Isomorphic Labs") Sir Demis Hassabis, and Google DeepMind Director Dr. John Jumper were co-awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their work developing [AlphaFold](/wiki/AlphaFold "AlphaFold"), a groundbreaking AI system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences. |
| 2025 | On February 6, [Mistral AI](/wiki/Mistral_AI "Mistral AI") releases Le Chat, an AI assistant able to answer up to 1,000 words per second.[[173]](#cite_note-175) |
| [Stargate UAE](/wiki/Stargate_UAE "Stargate UAE") invests to build Europe's largest AI data center in France.[[174]](#cite_note-176) |
| [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") |
| Amazon is training humanoid robots to deliver packages.[[175]](#cite_note-177) |
| [NLWeb](/wiki/NLWeb "NLWeb"), [Project Mariner](/wiki/Project_Mariner "Project Mariner"), and [Google Flow](/wiki/Google_Flow "Google Flow") launch. |
| On February 10 and 11, [France](/wiki/France "France") hosts the [Artificial Intelligence Action Summit](/wiki/Artificial_Intelligence_Action_Summit "Artificial Intelligence Action Summit").[[176]](#cite_note-178) 61 countries, including [China](/wiki/China "China"), [India](/wiki/India "India"), [Japan](/wiki/Japan "Japan"), France and [Canada](/wiki/Canada "Canada"), sign a declaration on "inclusive and sustainable" AI,[[177]](#cite_note-179) which the UK and US refused to sign.[[178]](#cite_note-180) |

title: History of artificial intelligence - Wikipedia
content:
The history of artificial intelligence (AI) began in antiquity, with myths, stories, and rumors of artificial beings endowed with intelligence or consciousness by master craftsmen. The study of logic and formal reasoning from antiquity to the present led directly to the invention of the programmable digital computer in the 1940s, a machine based on abstract mathematical reasoning. The **history of artificial intelligence** (**[AI](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence")**) began in [antiquity](/wiki/Ancient_history "Ancient history"), with myths, stories, and rumors of artificial beings endowed with intelligence or consciousness by master craftsmen. The study of logic and formal reasoning from antiquity to the present led directly to the invention of the [programmable digital computer](/wiki/Computer "Computer") in the 1940s, a machine based on abstract mathematical reasoning. This device and the ideas behind it inspired scientists to begin discussing the possibility of building an [electronic brain](/wiki/Electronic_brain "Electronic brain").

The field of AI research was founded at a [workshop](/wiki/Dartmouth_workshop "Dartmouth workshop") held on the campus of [Dartmouth College](/wiki/Dartmouth_College "Dartmouth College") in 1956.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplanHaenlein2018-1) Attendees of the workshop became the leaders of AI research for decades. Many of them predicted that machines as intelligent as humans would exist within a generation. The [U.S. government](/wiki/DARPA "DARPA") provided millions of dollars with the hope of making this vision come true.[[2]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist1994143–156-2)

Eventually, it became obvious that researchers had grossly underestimated the difficulty of this feat.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist1994144–152-3) In 1974, criticism from [James Lighthill](/wiki/James_Lighthill "James Lighthill") and pressure from the U.S.A. Congress led the U.S. and [British Governments](/wiki/British_Government "British Government") to stop funding undirected research into artificial intelligence. Seven years later, a visionary initiative by the [Japanese Government](/wiki/Japanese_Government "Japanese Government") and the success of [expert systems](/wiki/Expert_system "Expert system") reinvigorated investment in AI, and by the late 1980s, the industry had grown into a billion-dollar enterprise. However, investors' enthusiasm waned in the 1990s, and the field was criticized in the press and avoided by industry (a period known as an "[AI winter](/wiki/AI_winter "AI winter")"). Nevertheless, research and funding continued to grow under other names.

In the early 2000s, [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning") was applied to a wide range of problems in academia and industry. The success was due to the availability of powerful computer hardware, the collection of immense data sets, and the application of solid mathematical methods. Soon after, [deep learning](/wiki/Deep_learning "Deep learning") proved to be a breakthrough technology, eclipsing all other methods. The [transformer architecture](/wiki/Transformer_(deep_learning_architecture) "Transformer (deep learning architecture)") debuted in 2017 and was used to produce impressive [generative AI](/wiki/Generative_AI "Generative AI") applications, amongst other use cases.

Investment in AI [boomed](/wiki/AI_boom "AI boom") in the 2020s. The recent AI boom, initiated by the development of transformer architecture, led to the rapid scaling and public releases of [large language models](/wiki/Large_language_models "Large language models") (LLMs) like [ChatGPT](/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT"). These models exhibit human-like traits of knowledge, attention, and creativity, and have been integrated into various sectors, fueling exponential investment in AI. However, concerns about the potential risks and [ethical implications of advanced AI](/wiki/Ethics_of_artificial_intelligence "Ethics of artificial intelligence") have also emerged, causing debate about the future of AI and its impact on society.

## Precursors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Precursors")]

### Mythical, fictional, and speculative precursors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mythical, fictional, and speculative precursors")]

#### Myth and legend

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Myth and legend")]

In [Greek mythology](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology"), [Talos](/wiki/Talos "Talos") was a creature made of bronze who acted as guardian for the [island of Crete](/wiki/Crete "Crete"). He would throw boulders at the ships of invaders and would complete 3 circuits around the island's perimeter daily.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERhodios2007Book_4,_the_Talos_episode-4) According to [pseudo-Apollodorus](/wiki/Pseudo-Apollodorus "Pseudo-Apollodorus")' *[Bibliotheke](/wiki/Bibliotheca_(Pseudo-Apollodorus) "Bibliotheca (Pseudo-Apollodorus)")*, Hephaestus forged Talos with the aid of a cyclops and presented the [automaton](/wiki/Automaton "Automaton") as a gift to [Minos](/wiki/Minos "Minos").[[5]](#cite_note-5) In the [Argonautica](/wiki/Argonautica "Argonautica"), [Jason](/wiki/Jason "Jason") and the [Argonauts](/wiki/Argonauts "Argonauts") defeated Talos by removing a plug near his foot, causing the vital [ichor](/wiki/Ichor "Ichor") to flow out from his body and rendering him lifeless.[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERhodios2007-6)

[Pygmalion](/wiki/Pygmalion_(mythology) "Pygmalion (mythology)") was a legendary king and sculptor of Greek mythology, famously represented in [Ovid](/wiki/Ovid "Ovid")'s *[Metamorphoses](/wiki/Metamorphoses "Metamorphoses")*. In the 10th book of Ovid's narrative poem, Pygmalion becomes disgusted with women when he witnesses the way in which the [Propoetides](/wiki/Propoetides "Propoetides") prostitute themselves. Despite this, he makes offerings at the temple of Venus asking the goddess to bring to him a woman just like a statue he carved.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMorford2007-7)

#### Medieval legends of artificial beings

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Medieval legends of artificial beings")]

In *Of the Nature of Things*, the Swiss alchemist [Paracelsus](/wiki/Paracelsus "Paracelsus") describes a procedure that he claims can fabricate an "artificial man". By placing the "sperm of a man" in horse dung, and feeding it the "Arcanum of Mans blood" after 40 days, the concoction will become a living infant.[[8]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELinden2003-8)

The earliest written account regarding golem-making is found in the writings of [Eleazar ben Judah of Worms](/wiki/Eleazar_of_Worms "Eleazar of Worms") in the early 13th century.[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKressel2015-9) During the Middle Ages, it was believed that the animation of a [Golem](/wiki/Golem "Golem") could be achieved by insertion of a piece of paper with any of God's names on it, into the mouth of the clay figure.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJewish_EncyclopediaGOLEM-10) Unlike legendary automata like [Brazen Heads](/wiki/Brazen_head "Brazen head"),[[11]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist199438-11) a [Golem](/wiki/Golem "Golem") was unable to speak.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTETalmudSanhedrin_65b-12)

*[Takwin](/wiki/Takwin "Takwin")*, the artificial creation of life, was a frequent topic of [Ismaili](/wiki/Ismaili "Ismaili") alchemical manuscripts, especially those attributed to [Jabir ibn Hayyan](/wiki/Jabir_ibn_Hayyan "Jabir ibn Hayyan"). Islamic alchemists attempted to create a broad range of life through their work, ranging from plants to animals.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEO'Connor1994-13)

In [*Faust: The Second Part of the Tragedy*](/wiki/Faust,_Part_Two "Faust, Part Two") by [Johann Wolfgang von Goethe](/wiki/Johann_Wolfgang_von_Goethe "Johann Wolfgang von Goethe"), an alchemically fabricated [homunculus](/wiki/Homunculus "Homunculus"), destined to live forever in the flask in which he was made, endeavors to be born into a full human body. Upon the initiation of this transformation, however, the flask shatters and the homunculus dies.[[14]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoethe1890-14)

#### Modern fiction

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Modern fiction")]

Main article: [Artificial intelligence in fiction](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_in_fiction "Artificial intelligence in fiction")

By the 19th century, ideas about artificial men and thinking machines became a popular theme in fiction. Notable works like [Mary Shelley](/wiki/Mary_Shelley "Mary Shelley")'s *[Frankenstein](/wiki/Frankenstein "Frankenstein")* and [Karel Čapek](/wiki/Karel_%C4%8Capek "Karel Čapek")'s *[R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)](/wiki/R.U.R._(Rossum%27s_Universal_Robots) "R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)")*[[15]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck200417–25-15) explored the concept of artificial life. Speculative essays, such as [Samuel Butler](/wiki/Samuel_Butler_(novelist) "Samuel Butler (novelist)")'s "[Darwin among the Machines](/wiki/Darwin_among_the_Machines "Darwin among the Machines")",[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEButler1863-16) and [Edgar Allan Poe's](/wiki/Edgar_Allan_Poe "Edgar Allan Poe") "[Maelzel's Chess Player](/wiki/Maelzel%27s_Chess_Player "Maelzel's Chess Player")"[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist199465-17) reflected society's growing interest in machines with artificial intelligence. AI remains a common topic in science fiction today.[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaveDihal2019-18)

#### Automata

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Automata")]

Main article: [Automaton](/wiki/Automaton "Automaton")

Realistic humanoid [automata](/wiki/Automata "Automata") were built by craftsman from many civilizations, including [Yan Shi](/wiki/Yan_Shi "Yan Shi"),[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENeedham198653-19) [Hero of Alexandria](/wiki/Hero_of_Alexandria "Hero of Alexandria"),[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck20046-20) [Al-Jazari](/wiki/Al-Jazari "Al-Jazari"),[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENick2005-21) [Haroun al-Rashid](/wiki/Haroun_al-Rashid "Haroun al-Rashid"),[[22]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck200410-22) [Jacques de Vaucanson](/wiki/Jacques_de_Vaucanson "Jacques de Vaucanson"),[[23]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist199440-23)[[24]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck200416-24) [Leonardo Torres y Quevedo](/wiki/Leonardo_Torres_y_Quevedo "Leonardo Torres y Quevedo"),[[25]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck200459–62-25) [Pierre Jaquet-Droz](/wiki/Pierre_Jaquet-Droz "Pierre Jaquet-Droz") and [Wolfgang von Kempelen](/wiki/Wolfgang_von_Kempelen "Wolfgang von Kempelen").[[26]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck200417-26)[[27]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELevitt2000-27)

The oldest known automata were the [sacred statues](/wiki/Cult_image "Cult image") of [ancient Egypt](/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt") and [Greece](/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece").[[28]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist199430-28)[[29]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier19931-29) The faithful believed that craftsman had imbued these figures with very real minds, capable of wisdom and emotion—[Hermes Trismegistus](/wiki/Hermes_Trismegistus "Hermes Trismegistus") wrote that "by discovering the true nature of the gods, man has been able to reproduce it".[[30]](#cite_note-30) English scholar [Alexander Neckham](/wiki/Alexander_Neckham "Alexander Neckham") asserted that the Ancient Roman poet [Virgil](/wiki/Virgil "Virgil") had built a palace with automaton statues.[[31]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECaveDihalDillon202056-31)

During the early modern period, these legendary automata were said to possess the magical ability to answer questions put to them. The late medieval alchemist and proto-Protestant [Roger Bacon](/wiki/Roger_Bacon "Roger Bacon") was purported to have fabricated a [brazen head](/wiki/Brazen_head "Brazen head"), having developed a legend of having been a wizard.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEButler1979-32)[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPorterfield2006136-33) These legends were similar to the Norse myth of the Head of [Mímir](/wiki/M%C3%ADmir "Mímir"). According to legend, Mímir was known for his intellect and wisdom, and was beheaded in the [Æsir-Vanir War](/wiki/%C3%86sir-Vanir_War "Æsir-Vanir War"). [Odin](/wiki/Odin "Odin") is said to have "embalmed" the head with herbs and spoke incantations over it such that Mímir's head remained able to speak wisdom to Odin. Odin then kept the head near him for counsel.[[34]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHollander1991-34)

### Formal reasoning

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Formal reasoning")]

Artificial intelligence is based on the assumption that the process of human thought can be mechanized. The study of mechanical—or "formal"—reasoning has a long history. [Chinese](/wiki/Logic_in_China "Logic in China"), [Indian](/wiki/Indian_Logic "Indian Logic") and [Greek](/wiki/History_of_Logic#Logic_in_the_West "History of Logic") philosophers all developed structured methods of formal deduction by the first millennium BCE. Their ideas were developed over the centuries by philosophers such as [Aristotle](/wiki/Aristotle "Aristotle") (who gave a formal analysis of the [syllogism](/wiki/Syllogism "Syllogism")),[[35]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20216_&_7-35) [Euclid](/wiki/Euclid "Euclid") (whose *[Elements](/wiki/Euclid%27s_Elements "Euclid's Elements")* was a model of formal reasoning), [al-Khwārizmī](/wiki/Muhammad_ibn_Musa_al-Khwarizmi "Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi") (who developed [algebra](/wiki/Algebra "Algebra") and gave his name to the word *[algorithm](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm")*) and European [scholastic](/wiki/Scholasticism "Scholasticism") philosophers such as [William of Ockham](/wiki/William_of_Ockham "William of Ockham") and [Duns Scotus](/wiki/Duns_Scotus "Duns Scotus").[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerlinski2000-36)

Spanish philosopher [Ramon Llull](/wiki/Ramon_Llull "Ramon Llull") (1232–1315) developed several *logical machines* devoted to the production of knowledge by logical means;[[37]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarreras_y_Artau2018-37)[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20216-38) Llull described his machines as mechanical entities that could combine basic and undeniable truths by simple logical operations, produced by the machine by mechanical meanings, in such ways as to produce all the possible knowledge.[[39]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonner2007-39) Llull's work had a great influence on [Gottfried Leibniz](/wiki/Gottfried_Leibniz "Gottfried Leibniz"), who redeveloped his ideas.[[40]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonner198557–71-40)

In the 17th century, [Leibniz](/wiki/Gottfried_Leibniz "Gottfried Leibniz"), [Thomas Hobbes](/wiki/Thomas_Hobbes "Thomas Hobbes") and [René Descartes](/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes "René Descartes") explored the possibility that all rational thought could be made as systematic as algebra or geometry.[[41]](#cite_note-41) [Hobbes](/wiki/Hobbes "Hobbes") famously wrote in [*Leviathan*](/wiki/Leviathan_(Hobbes_book) "Leviathan (Hobbes book)"): "For *reason* ... is nothing but *reckoning*, that is adding and subtracting".[[42]](#cite_note-42) [Leibniz](/wiki/Gottfried_Leibniz "Gottfried Leibniz") envisioned a universal language of reasoning, the *[characteristica universalis](/wiki/Characteristica_universalis "Characteristica universalis")*, which would reduce argumentation to calculation so that "there would be no more need of disputation between two philosophers than between two accountants. For it would suffice to take their pencils in hand, down to their slates, and to say each other (with a friend as witness, if they liked): *Let us calculate*."[[43]](#cite_note-43) These philosophers had begun to articulate the [physical symbol system](/wiki/Physical_symbol_system "Physical symbol system") hypothesis that would guide AI research.

The study of [mathematical logic](/wiki/Mathematical_logic "Mathematical logic") provided the essential breakthrough that made artificial intelligence seem plausible. The foundations had been set by such works as [Boole](/wiki/George_Boole "George Boole")'s *[The Laws of Thought](/wiki/The_Laws_of_Thought "The Laws of Thought")* and [Frege](/wiki/Frege "Frege")'s *[Begriffsschrift](/wiki/Begriffsschrift "Begriffsschrift")*.[[44]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20218-44) Building on [Frege](/wiki/Frege "Frege")'s system, [Russell](/wiki/Bertrand_Russell "Bertrand Russell") and [Whitehead](/wiki/Alfred_North_Whitehead "Alfred North Whitehead") presented a formal treatment of the foundations of mathematics in their masterpiece, the *[Principia Mathematica](/wiki/Principia_Mathematica "Principia Mathematica")* in 1913. Inspired by [Russell](/wiki/Bertrand_Russell "Bertrand Russell")'s success, [David Hilbert](/wiki/Hilbert%27s_program "Hilbert's program") challenged mathematicians of the 1920s and 30s to answer this fundamental question: "can all of mathematical reasoning be formalized?"[[36]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerlinski2000-36) His question was answered by [Gödel](/wiki/Kurt_G%C3%B6del "Kurt Gödel")'s [incompleteness proof](/wiki/G%C3%B6del%27s_incompleteness_theorems "Gödel's incompleteness theorems"),[[45]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20219-45) [Turing](/wiki/Alan_Turing "Alan Turing")'s [machine](/wiki/Turing_machine "Turing machine")[[45]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20219-45) and [Church](/wiki/Alonzo_Church "Alonzo Church")'s [Lambda calculus](/wiki/Lambda_calculus "Lambda calculus").[[a]](#cite_note-47)

Their answer was surprising in two ways. First, they proved that there were, in fact, limits to what mathematical logic could accomplish. But second (and more important for AI) their work suggested that, within these limits, *any* form of mathematical reasoning could be mechanized. The [Church-Turing thesis](/wiki/Church-Turing_thesis "Church-Turing thesis") implied that a mechanical device, shuffling symbols as simple as *0* and *1*, could imitate any conceivable process of mathematical deduction.[[45]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20219-45) The key insight was the [Turing machine](/wiki/Turing_machine "Turing machine")—a simple theoretical construct that captured the essence of abstract symbol manipulation.[[48]](#cite_note-49) This invention would inspire a handful of scientists to begin discussing the possibility of thinking machines.

### Computer science

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Computer science")]

Main articles: [History of computer hardware](/wiki/History_of_computer_hardware "History of computer hardware") and [History of computer science](/wiki/History_of_computer_science "History of computer science")

Calculating machines were designed or built in antiquity and throughout history by many people, including [Gottfried Leibniz](/wiki/Gottfried_Leibniz#Information_technology "Gottfried Leibniz"),[[38]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig20216-38)[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECouturat1901-50) [Joseph Marie Jacquard](/wiki/Joseph_Marie_Jacquard "Joseph Marie Jacquard"),[[50]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202115-51) [Charles Babbage](/wiki/Charles_Babbage "Charles Babbage"),[[50]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202115-51)[[51]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist199467-52) [Percy Ludgate](/wiki/Percy_Ludgate "Percy Ludgate"),[[52]](#cite_note-53) [Leonardo Torres Quevedo](/wiki/Leonardo_Torres_Quevedo "Leonardo Torres Quevedo"),[[53]](#cite_note-54) [Vannevar Bush](/wiki/Vannevar_Bush "Vannevar Bush"),[[54]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERandall198213,_16–17-55) and others. [Ada Lovelace](/wiki/Ada_Lovelace "Ada Lovelace") speculated that Babbage's machine was "a thinking or ... reasoning machine", but warned "It is desirable to guard against the possibility of exaggerated ideas that arise as to the powers" of the machine.[[55]](#cite_note-56)[[56]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMenabreaLovelace1843-57)

The first modern computers were the massive machines of the [Second World War](/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") (such as [Konrad Zuse](/wiki/Konrad_Zuse "Konrad Zuse")'s [Z3](/wiki/Z3_(computer) "Z3 (computer)"), [Alan Turing](/wiki/Alan_Turing "Alan Turing")'s [Heath Robinson](/wiki/Heath_Robinson_machine "Heath Robinson machine") and [Colossus](/wiki/Colossus_computer "Colossus computer"), [Atanasoff](/wiki/John_Vincent_Atanasoff "John Vincent Atanasoff") and [Berry](/wiki/Clifford_Berry "Clifford Berry")'s [ABC](/wiki/Atanasoff%E2%80%93Berry_computer "Atanasoff–Berry computer"), and [ENIAC](/wiki/ENIAC "ENIAC") at the [University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania")).[[57]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202114-58) [ENIAC](/wiki/ENIAC "ENIAC") was based on the theoretical foundation laid by [Alan Turing](/wiki/Alan_Turing "Alan Turing") and developed by [John von Neumann](/wiki/John_von_Neumann "John von Neumann"),[[58]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck200476–80-59) and proved to be the most influential.[[57]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202114-58)

## Birth of artificial intelligence (1941–1956)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Birth of artificial intelligence (1941–1956)")]

The earliest research into thinking machines was inspired by a confluence of ideas that became prevalent in the late 1930s, 1940s, and early 1950s. Recent research in [neurology](/wiki/Neurology "Neurology") had shown that the brain was an electrical network of [neurons](/wiki/Neuron "Neuron") that fired in all-or-nothing pulses. [Norbert Wiener](/wiki/Norbert_Wiener "Norbert Wiener")'s [cybernetics](/wiki/Cybernetic "Cybernetic") described control and stability in electrical networks. [Claude Shannon](/wiki/Claude_Shannon "Claude Shannon")'s [information theory](/wiki/Information_theory "Information theory") described digital signals (i.e., all-or-nothing signals). [Alan Turing](/wiki/Alan_Turing "Alan Turing")'s [theory of computation](/wiki/Theory_of_computation "Theory of computation") showed that any form of computation could be described digitally. The close relationship between these ideas suggested that it might be possible to construct an "electronic brain".

In the 1940s and 50s, a handful of scientists from a variety of fields (mathematics, psychology, engineering, economics and political science) explored several research directions that would be vital to later AI research.[[59]](#cite_note-60) Alan Turing was among the first people to seriously investigate the theoretical possibility of "machine intelligence".[[60]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECopeland2004-61) The field of "[artificial intelligence research](/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence")" was founded as an academic discipline in 1956.[[61]](#cite_note-Dartmouth_workshop-62)

### Turing test

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Turing test")]

Main article: [Turing test](/wiki/Turing_test "Turing test")

In 1950 Turing published a landmark paper "[Computing Machinery and Intelligence](/wiki/Computing_Machinery_and_Intelligence "Computing Machinery and Intelligence")", in which he speculated about the possibility of creating machines that think.[[63]](#cite_note-64)[[b]](#cite_note-65) In the paper, he noted that "thinking" is difficult to define and devised his famous [Turing test](/wiki/Turing_Test "Turing Test"): If a machine could carry on a conversation (over a [teleprinter](/wiki/Teleprinter "Teleprinter")) that was indistinguishable from a conversation with a human being, then it was reasonable to say that the machine was "thinking".[[64]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENewquist199492–98-66) This simplified version of the problem allowed Turing to argue convincingly that a "thinking machine" was at least *plausible* and the paper answered all the most common objections to the proposition.[[65]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig2021981-67) The Turing test was the first serious proposal in the [philosophy of artificial intelligence](/wiki/Philosophy_of_artificial_intelligence "Philosophy of artificial intelligence").

### Neuroscience and Hebbian theory

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Neuroscience and Hebbian theory")]

[Donald Hebb](/wiki/Donald_Hebb "Donald Hebb") was a Canadian psychologist whose work laid the foundation for modern neuroscience, particularly in understanding learning, memory, and neural plasticity. His most influential book, *The Organization of Behavior* (1949), introduced the concept of Hebbian learning, often summarized as "cells that fire together wire together."[[66]](#cite_note-68)

Hebb began formulating the foundational ideas for this book in the early 1940s, particularly during his time at the Yerkes Laboratories of Primate Biology from 1942 to 1947. He made extensive notes between June 1944 and March 1945 and sent a complete draft to his mentor Karl Lashley in 1946. The manuscript for *The Organization of Behavior* wasn’t published until 1949. The delay was due to various factors, including World War II and shifts in academic focus. By the time it was published, several of his peers had already published related ideas, making Hebb's work seem less groundbreaking at first glance. However, his synthesis of psychological and neurophysiological principles became a cornerstone of neuroscience and machine learning.[[67]](#cite_note-69)[[68]](#cite_note-70)

### Artificial neural networks

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Artificial neural networks")]

[Walter Pitts](/wiki/Walter_Pitts "Walter Pitts") and [Warren McCulloch](/wiki/Warren_Sturgis_McCulloch "Warren Sturgis McCulloch") analyzed networks of idealized [artificial neurons](/wiki/Artificial_neuron "Artificial neuron") and showed how they might perform simple logical functions in 1943. They were the first to describe what later researchers would call a [neural network](/wiki/Artificial_neural_network "Artificial neural network").[[69]](#cite_note-71) The paper was influenced by Turing's paper "[On Computable Numbers](/wiki/Turing%27s_proof "Turing's proof")" from 1936 using similar two-state boolean 'neurons', but was the first to apply it to neuronal function.[[60]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECopeland2004-61) One of the students inspired by Pitts and McCulloch was [Marvin Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") who was a 24-year-old graduate student at the time. In 1951 Minsky and Dean Edmonds built the first neural net machine, the [SNARC](/wiki/Stochastic_Neural_Analog_Reinforcement_Calculator "Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator").[[70]](#cite_note-72) Minsky would later become one of the most important leaders and innovators in AI.

### Cybernetic robots

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Cybernetic robots")]

Experimental robots such as [W. Grey Walter](/wiki/W._Grey_Walter "W. Grey Walter")'s [turtles](/wiki/Turtle_(robot) "Turtle (robot)") and the [Johns Hopkins Beast](/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_Beast "Johns Hopkins Beast"), were built in the 1950s. These machines did not use computers, digital electronics, or symbolic reasoning; they were controlled entirely by analog circuitry.[[71]](#cite_note-73)

### Game AI

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Game AI")]

In 1951, using the [Ferranti Mark 1](/wiki/Ferranti_Mark_1 "Ferranti Mark 1") machine of the [University of Manchester](/wiki/University_of_Manchester "University of Manchester"), [Christopher Strachey](/wiki/Christopher_Strachey "Christopher Strachey") wrote a checkers program[[72]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202117-74) and [Dietrich Prinz](/wiki/Dietrich_Prinz "Dietrich Prinz") wrote one for chess.[[73]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECopeland1999-75) [Arthur Samuel](/wiki/Arthur_Samuel_(computer_scientist) "Arthur Samuel (computer scientist)")'s checkers program, the subject of his 1959 paper "Some Studies in Machine Learning Using the Game of Checkers", eventually achieved sufficient skill to challenge a respectable amateur.[[74]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchaeffer1997Chapter_6-76) Samuel's program was among the first uses of what would later be called [machine learning](/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning").[[75]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202117,_19-77) [Game AI](/wiki/Game_AI "Game AI") would continue to be used as a measure of progress in AI throughout its history.

### Symbolic reasoning and the Logic Theorist

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Symbolic reasoning and the Logic Theorist")]

Main article: [Logic Theorist](/wiki/Logic_Theorist "Logic Theorist")

When access to [digital computers](/wiki/Digital_computer "Digital computer") became possible in the mid-fifties, a few scientists instinctively recognized that a machine that could manipulate numbers could also manipulate symbols and that the manipulation of symbols could well be the essence of human thought. This was a new approach to creating thinking machines.[[76]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck2004137–170-78)[[77]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199344–47-79)

In 1955, [Allen Newell](/wiki/Allen_Newell "Allen Newell") and future Nobel Laureate [Herbert A. Simon](/wiki/Herbert_A._Simon "Herbert A. Simon") created the "Logic Theorist", with help from [J. C. Shaw](/wiki/Cliff_Shaw "Cliff Shaw"). The program would eventually prove 38 of the first 52 theorems in [Russell](/wiki/Bertrand_Russell "Bertrand Russell") and [Whitehead](/wiki/Alfred_North_Whitehead "Alfred North Whitehead")'s *[Principia Mathematica](/wiki/Principia_Mathematica "Principia Mathematica")*, and find new and more elegant proofs for some.[[78]](#cite_note-80) Simon said that they had "solved the venerable [mind/body problem](/wiki/Mind/body_problem "Mind/body problem"), explaining how a system composed of matter can have the properties of mind."[[79]](#cite_note-81)[[c]](#cite_note-82) The symbolic reasoning paradigm they introduced would dominate AI research and funding until the middle 90s, as well as inspire the [cognitive revolution](/wiki/Cognitive_revolution "Cognitive revolution").

### Dartmouth Workshop

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Dartmouth Workshop")]

Main article: [Dartmouth workshop](/wiki/Dartmouth_workshop "Dartmouth workshop")

The Dartmouth workshop of 1956 was a pivotal event that marked the formal inception of AI as an academic discipline.[[61]](#cite_note-Dartmouth_workshop-62) It was organized by [Marvin Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") and [John McCarthy](/wiki/John_McCarthy_(computer_scientist) "John McCarthy (computer scientist)"), with the support of two senior scientists [Claude Shannon](/wiki/Claude_Shannon "Claude Shannon") and [Nathan Rochester](/wiki/Nathaniel_Rochester_(computer_scientist) "Nathaniel Rochester (computer scientist)") of [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM"). The proposal for the conference stated they intended to test the assertion that "every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it".[[80]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCarthyMinskyRochesterShannon1955-83)[[d]](#cite_note-86) The term "Artificial Intelligence" was introduced by John McCarthy at the workshop.[[e]](#cite_note-90) The participants included [Ray Solomonoff](/wiki/Ray_Solomonoff "Ray Solomonoff"), [Oliver Selfridge](/wiki/Oliver_Selfridge "Oliver Selfridge"), [Trenchard More](/wiki/Trenchard_More "Trenchard More"), [Arthur Samuel](/wiki/Arthur_Samuel_(computer_scientist) "Arthur Samuel (computer scientist)"), [Allen Newell](/wiki/Allen_Newell "Allen Newell") and [Herbert A. Simon](/wiki/Herbert_A._Simon "Herbert A. Simon"), all of whom would create important programs during the first decades of AI research.[[86]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck2004129–130-91)[[f]](#cite_note-92) At the workshop Newell and Simon debuted the "Logic Theorist".[[87]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck2004125-93) The workshop was the moment that AI gained its name, its mission, its first major success and its key players, and is widely considered the birth of AI.[[g]](#cite_note-95)

### Cognitive revolution

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Cognitive revolution")]

Main article: [cognitive revolution](/wiki/Cognitive_revolution "Cognitive revolution")

In the autumn of 1956, Newell and Simon also presented the Logic Theorist at a meeting of the Special Interest Group in Information Theory at the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") (MIT). At the same meeting, [Noam Chomsky](/wiki/Noam_Chomsky "Noam Chomsky") discussed his [generative grammar](/wiki/Generative_grammar "Generative grammar"), and [George Miller](/wiki/George_Armitage_Miller "George Armitage Miller") described his landmark paper "[The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two](/wiki/The_Magical_Number_Seven,_Plus_or_Minus_Two "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two")". Miller wrote "I left the symposium with a conviction, more intuitive than rational, that experimental psychology, theoretical linguistics, and the computer simulation of cognitive processes were all pieces from a larger whole."[[89]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2003-96)[[57]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202114-58)

This meeting was the beginning of the "[cognitive revolution](/wiki/Cognitive_revolution "Cognitive revolution")"—an interdisciplinary [paradigm shift](/wiki/Paradigm_shift "Paradigm shift") in psychology, philosophy, computer science and neuroscience. It inspired the creation of the sub-fields of [symbolic artificial intelligence](/wiki/Symbolic_artificial_intelligence "Symbolic artificial intelligence"), [generative linguistics](/wiki/Generative_linguistics "Generative linguistics"), [cognitive science](/wiki/Cognitive_science "Cognitive science"), [cognitive psychology](/wiki/Cognitive_psychology "Cognitive psychology"), [cognitive neuroscience](/wiki/Cognitive_neuroscience "Cognitive neuroscience") and the philosophical schools of [computationalism](/wiki/Computationalism "Computationalism") and [functionalism](/wiki/Functionalism_(philosophy) "Functionalism (philosophy)"). All these fields used related tools to model the mind and results discovered in one field were relevant to the others.

The cognitive approach allowed researchers to consider "mental objects" like thoughts, plans, goals, facts or memories, often analyzed using [high level symbols](/wiki/Physical_symbol_system "Physical symbol system") in functional networks. These objects had been forbidden as "unobservable" by earlier paradigms such as [behaviorism](/wiki/Behaviorism "Behaviorism").[[h]](#cite_note-98) Symbolic mental objects would become the major focus of AI research and funding for the next several decades.

## Early successes (1956–1974)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Early successes (1956–1974)")]

The programs developed in the years after the [Dartmouth Workshop](/wiki/Dartmouth_workshop "Dartmouth workshop") were, to most people, simply "astonishing":[[i]](#cite_note-101) computers were solving algebra word problems, proving theorems in geometry and learning to speak English. Few at the time would have believed that such "intelligent" behavior by machines was possible at all.[[93]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199352–107-102)[[94]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoravec19889-103)[[92]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202118-100) Researchers expressed an intense optimism in private and in print, predicting that a fully intelligent machine would be built in less than 20 years.[[95]](#cite_note-104) Government agencies like the [Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency](/wiki/Defense_Advanced_Research_Projects_Agency "Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency") (DARPA, then known as "ARPA") poured money into the field.[[96]](#cite_note-105) Artificial Intelligence laboratories were set up at a number of British and US universities in the latter 1950s and early 1960s.[[60]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECopeland2004-61)

### Approaches

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Approaches")]

There were many successful programs and new directions in the late 50s and 1960s. Among the most influential were these:

#### Reasoning, planning and problem solving as search

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Reasoning, planning and problem solving as search")]

Many early AI programs used the same basic [algorithm](/wiki/Algorithm "Algorithm"). To achieve some goal (like winning a game or proving a theorem), they proceeded step by step towards it (by making a move or a deduction) as if searching through a maze, [backtracking](/wiki/Backtracking "Backtracking") whenever they reached a dead end.[[97]](#cite_note-106) The principal difficulty was that, for many problems, the number of possible paths through the "maze" was astronomical (a situation known as a "[combinatorial explosion](/wiki/Combinatorial_explosion "Combinatorial explosion")"). Researchers would reduce the search space by using [heuristics](/wiki/Heuristics "Heuristics") that would eliminate paths that were unlikely to lead to a solution.[[98]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck2004246-107)

[Newell](/wiki/Allen_Newell "Allen Newell") and [Simon](/wiki/Herbert_A._Simon "Herbert A. Simon") tried to capture a general version of this algorithm in a program called the "[General Problem Solver](/wiki/General_Problem_Solver "General Problem Solver")".[[99]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck2004245–250-108)[[100]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202119,_106-109) Other "searching" programs were able to accomplish impressive tasks like solving problems in geometry and algebra, such as [Herbert Gelernter](/wiki/Herbert_Gelernter "Herbert Gelernter")'s Geometry Theorem Prover (1958)[[101]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202119-110) and Symbolic Automatic Integrator (SAINT), written by [Minsky's](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") student James Slagle in 1961.[[102]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199351–58,_65–66-111)[[103]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202120-112) Other programs searched through goals and subgoals to [plan actions](/w/index.php?title=Automatic_scheduling_and_planning&action=edit&redlink=1 "Automatic scheduling and planning (page does not exist)"), like the [STRIPS](/wiki/Stanford_Research_Institute_Problem_Solver "Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver") system developed at [Stanford](/wiki/Stanford "Stanford") to control the behavior of the robot [Shakey](/wiki/Shakey_the_Robot "Shakey the Robot").[[104]](#cite_note-113)

#### Natural language

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Natural language")]

An important goal of AI research is to allow computers to communicate in [natural languages](/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing") like English. An early success was [Daniel Bobrow](/wiki/Daniel_Bobrow "Daniel Bobrow")'s program [STUDENT](/wiki/STUDENT_(computer_program) "STUDENT (computer program)"), which could solve high school algebra word problems.[[105]](#cite_note-114)

A [semantic net](/wiki/Semantic_net "Semantic net") represents concepts (e.g. "house", "door") as nodes, and relations among concepts as links between the nodes (e.g. "has-a"). The first AI program to use a semantic net was written by Ross Quillian[[106]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199379–83-115) and the most successful (and controversial) version was [Roger Schank](/wiki/Roger_Schank "Roger Schank")'s [Conceptual dependency theory](/wiki/Conceptual_dependency_theory "Conceptual dependency theory").[[107]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993164–172-116)

[Joseph Weizenbaum](/wiki/Joseph_Weizenbaum "Joseph Weizenbaum")'s [ELIZA](/wiki/ELIZA "ELIZA") could carry out conversations that were so realistic that users occasionally were fooled into thinking they were communicating with a human being and not a computer program (see [ELIZA effect](/wiki/ELIZA_effect "ELIZA effect")). But in fact, ELIZA simply gave a [canned response](/wiki/Canned_response "Canned response") or repeated back what was said to it, rephrasing its response with a few grammar rules. ELIZA was the first [chatbot](/wiki/Chatbot "Chatbot").[[108]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcCorduck2004291–296-117)[[109]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993134–139-118)

#### Micro-worlds

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Micro-worlds")]

In the late 60s, [Marvin Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") and [Seymour Papert](/wiki/Seymour_Papert "Seymour Papert") of the [MIT](/wiki/MIT "MIT") AI Laboratory proposed that AI research should focus on artificially simple situations known as micro-worlds.[[j]](#cite_note-119) They pointed out that in successful sciences like physics, basic principles were often best understood using simplified models like frictionless planes or perfectly rigid bodies. Much of the research focused on a "[blocks world](/wiki/Blocks_world "Blocks world")," which consists of colored blocks of various shapes and sizes arrayed on a flat surface.[[110]](#cite_note-Blocks_world-120)

This paradigm led to innovative work in [machine vision](/wiki/Machine_vision "Machine vision") by [Gerald Sussman](/wiki/Gerald_Sussman "Gerald Sussman"), Adolfo Guzman, [David Waltz](/wiki/David_Waltz "David Waltz") (who invented "[constraint propagation](/wiki/Constraint_propagation "Constraint propagation")"), and especially [Patrick Winston](/wiki/Patrick_Winston "Patrick Winston"). At the same time, Minsky and Papert built a robot arm that could stack blocks, bringing the blocks world to life. [Terry Winograd](/wiki/Terry_Winograd "Terry Winograd")'s [SHRDLU](/wiki/SHRDLU "SHRDLU") could communicate in ordinary English sentences about the micro-world, plan operations and execute them.[[110]](#cite_note-Blocks_world-120)

#### Perceptrons and early neural networks

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Perceptrons and early neural networks")]

Main article: [Perceptron](/wiki/Perceptron "Perceptron")

In the 1960s funding was primarily directed towards laboratories researching [symbolic AI](/wiki/Symbolic_artificial_intelligence "Symbolic artificial intelligence"), however several people still pursued research in neural networks.

The [perceptron](/wiki/Perceptron "Perceptron"), a single-layer [neural network](/wiki/Artificial_neural_network "Artificial neural network") was introduced in 1958 by [Frank Rosenblatt](/wiki/Frank_Rosenblatt "Frank Rosenblatt")[[111]](#cite_note-121) (who had been a schoolmate of [Marvin Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") at the [Bronx High School of Science](/wiki/Bronx_High_School_of_Science "Bronx High School of Science")).[[112]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993102-122) Like most AI researchers, he was optimistic about their power, predicting that a perceptron "may eventually be able to learn, make decisions, and translate languages."[[113]](#cite_note-123) Rosenblatt was primarily funded by [Office of Naval Research](/wiki/Office_of_Naval_Research "Office of Naval Research").[[114]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERosenblatt1962-124)

[Bernard Widrow](/wiki/Bernard_Widrow "Bernard Widrow") and his student [Ted Hoff](/wiki/Marcian_Hoff "Marcian Hoff") built [ADALINE](/wiki/ADALINE "ADALINE") (1960) and [MADALINE](/wiki/ADALINE "ADALINE") (1962), which had up to 1000 adjustable weights.[[115]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202120–21-125)[[116]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWidrowLehr1990-126) A group at [Stanford Research Institute](/wiki/SRI_International "SRI International") led by [Charles A. Rosen](/wiki/Charles_Rosen_(scientist) "Charles Rosen (scientist)") and Alfred E. (Ted) Brain built two neural network machines named MINOS I (1960) and II (1963), mainly funded by [U.S. Army Signal Corps](/wiki/United_States_Army_Signal_Corps "United States Army Signal Corps"). MINOS II[[117]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERosenNilssonAdams1965-127) had 6600 adjustable weights,[[118]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson1984-128) and was controlled with an [SDS 910 computer](/wiki/SDS_9_Series "SDS 9 Series") in a configuration named MINOS III (1968), which could classify symbols on army maps, and recognize hand-printed characters on [Fortran](/wiki/Fortran "Fortran") [coding sheets](/wiki/Computer_programming_in_the_punched_card_era "Computer programming in the punched card era").[[119]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHartNilssonPerraultMitchell2003-129)[[120]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENielson2005-130) Most of neural network research during this early period involved building and using bespoke hardware, rather than simulation on digital computers.[[k]](#cite_note-132)

However, partly due to lack of results and partly due to competition from [symbolic AI](/wiki/Symbolic_AI "Symbolic AI") research, the MINOS project ran out of funding in 1966. Rosenblatt failed to secure continued funding in the 1960s.[[121]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlazaran_Rodriguez1991-131) In 1969 research came to a sudden halt with the publication of [Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") and [Papert's](/wiki/Seymour_Papert "Seymour Papert") 1969 book *[Perceptrons](/wiki/Perceptrons_(book) "Perceptrons (book)")*.[[122]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMinskyPapert1969-133) It suggested that there were severe limitations to what perceptrons could do and that Rosenblatt's predictions had been grossly exaggerated. The effect of the book was that virtually no research was funded in [connectionism](/wiki/Connectionism "Connectionism") for 10 years.[[123]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202122-134) The competition for government funding ended with the victory of symbolic AI approaches over neural networks.[[120]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENielson2005-130)[[121]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlazaran_Rodriguez1991-131)

Minsky (who had worked on [SNARC](/wiki/Stochastic_Neural_Analog_Reinforcement_Calculator "Stochastic Neural Analog Reinforcement Calculator")) became a staunch objector to pure connectionist AI. [Widrow](/wiki/Bernard_Widrow "Bernard Widrow") (who had worked on [ADALINE](/wiki/ADALINE "ADALINE")) turned to adaptive signal processing. The [SRI](/wiki/SRI_International "SRI International") group (which worked on MINOS) turned to symbolic AI and robotics.[[120]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENielson2005-130)[[121]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlazaran_Rodriguez1991-131)

The main problem was the inability to train multilayered networks (versions of [backpropagation](/wiki/Backpropagation "Backpropagation") had already been used in other fields but it was unknown to these researchers).[[124]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmidhuber2022-135)[[123]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202122-134) The AI community became aware of backpropogation in the 80s,[[125]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussellNorvig202124-136) and, in the 21st century, neural networks would become enormously successful, fulfilling all of Rosenblatt's optimistic predictions. Rosenblatt did not live to see this, however, as he died in a boating accident in 1971.[[126]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993105-137)

### Optimism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Optimism")]

The first generation of AI researchers made these predictions about their work:

* 1958, [H. A. Simon](/wiki/H._A._Simon "H. A. Simon") and [Allen Newell](/wiki/Allen_Newell "Allen Newell"): "within ten years a digital computer will be the world's chess champion" and "within ten years a digital computer will discover and prove an important new mathematical theorem."[[127]](#cite_note-138)
* 1965, H. A. Simon: "machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can do."[[128]](#cite_note-139)
* 1967, [Marvin Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky"): "Within a generation... the problem of creating 'artificial intelligence' will substantially be solved."[[129]](#cite_note-140)
* 1970, Marvin Minsky (in [*Life* magazine](/wiki/Life_magazine "Life magazine")): "In from three to eight years we will have a machine with the general intelligence of an average human being."[[130]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDarrach1970-141)[[l]](#cite_note-144)

### Financing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Financing")]

In June 1963, [MIT](/wiki/MIT "MIT") received a $2.2 million grant from the newly created Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA, later known as [DARPA](/wiki/DARPA "DARPA")). The money was used to fund [project MAC](/wiki/Project_MAC "Project MAC") which subsumed the "AI Group" founded by [Minsky](/wiki/Marvin_Minsky "Marvin Minsky") and [McCarthy](/wiki/John_McCarthy_(computer_scientist) "John McCarthy (computer scientist)") five years earlier. DARPA continued to provide $3 million each year until the 70s.[[133]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199364–65-145) DARPA made similar grants to [Newell](/wiki/Allen_Newell "Allen Newell") and [Simon's](/wiki/Herbert_A._Simon "Herbert A. Simon") program at [Carnegie Mellon University](/wiki/Carnegie_Mellon_University "Carnegie Mellon University") and to [Stanford University](/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University")'s [AI Lab](/wiki/Stanford_AI_Lab "Stanford AI Lab"), founded by [John McCarthy](/wiki/John_McCarthy_(computer_scientist) "John McCarthy (computer scientist)") in 1963.[[134]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199394-146) Another important AI laboratory was established at [Edinburgh University](/wiki/Edinburgh_University "Edinburgh University") by [Donald Michie](/wiki/Donald_Michie "Donald Michie") in 1965.[[135]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHowe1994-147) These four institutions would continue to be the main centers of AI research and funding in academia for many years.[[136]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199351-148)[[m]](#cite_note-150)

The money was given with few strings attached: [J. C. R. Licklider](/wiki/J._C._R._Licklider "J. C. R. Licklider"), then the director of ARPA, believed that his organization should "fund people, not projects!" and allowed researchers to pursue whatever directions might interest them.[[138]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier199365-151) This created a freewheeling atmosphere at MIT that gave birth to the [hacker culture](/wiki/Hacker_culture "Hacker culture"),[[139]](#cite_note-152) but this "hands off" approach did not last.

## First AI winter (1974–1980)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: First AI winter (1974–1980)")]

In the 1970s, AI was subject to critiques and financial setbacks. AI researchers had failed to appreciate the difficulty of the problems they faced. Their tremendous optimism had raised public expectations impossibly high, and when the promised results failed to materialize, funding targeted at AI was severely reduced.[[140]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993163–196-153) The lack of success indicated the techniques being used by AI researchers at the time were insufficient to achieve their goals.[[141]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDreyfus1972-154)[[142]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELighthill1973-155)

These setbacks did not affect the growth and progress of the field, however. The funding cuts only impacted a handful of major laboratories[[143]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaigh2023-156) and the critiques were largely ignored.[[144]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993143-157) General public interest in the field continued to grow,[[143]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaigh2023-156) the number of researchers increased dramatically,[[143]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaigh2023-156) and new ideas were explored in [logic programming](/wiki/Logic_programming "Logic programming"), [commonsense reasoning](/wiki/Commonsense_reasoning "Commonsense reasoning") and many other areas. Historian Thomas Haigh argued in 2023 that there was no winter,[[143]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHaigh2023-156) and AI researcher [Nils Nilsson](/wiki/Nils_John_Nilsson "Nils John Nilsson") described this period as the most "exciting" time to work in AI.[[145]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilsson20091-158)

### Problems

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=History_of_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Problems")]

In the early seventies, the capabilities of AI programs were limited. Even the most impressive could only handle trivial versions of the problems they were supposed to solve;[[n]](#cite_note-160) all the programs were, in some sense, "toys".[[147]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993146-161) AI researchers had begun to run into several limits that would be only conquered decades later, and others that still stymie the field in the 2020s:

* **[Limited computer power](/wiki/Moore%27s_law "Moore's law")**: There was not enough memory or processing speed to accomplish anything truly useful.[[o]](#cite_note-163) For example: Ross Quillian's successful work on natural language was demonstrated with a vocabulary of only 20 words, because that was all that would fit in memory.[[149]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrevier1993146–148-164) [Hans Moravec](/wiki/Hans_Moravec "Hans Moravec") argued in 1976 that computers were still millions of times too weak to exhibit intelligence. He suggested an analogy: artificial intelligence requires computer power in the same way that aircraft require [horsepower](/wiki/Horsepower "Horsepower"). Below a certain threshold, it's impossible, but, as power [increases](/wiki/Moore%27s_law "Moore's law"), eventually it could become easy. "With enough horsepower," he wrote, "anything will fly".[[150]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoravec1976-165)[[p]](#cite_note-167)
